lead.headline: Home-computer price fight moves to the family counter
lead.dek: Commodore, Texas Instruments, Atari, and IBM-compatible software all compete for attention as February shoppers compare game libraries, BASIC, memory, and office promises.
lead.body: By mid-February 1983, the home-computer boom was becoming a shelf-by-shelf argument. Commodore 64 advertising leaned on memory and color, TI-99/4A promotions kept pressure on price, Atari remained tied to both games and BASIC, and IBM PC software such as Lotus 1-2-3 gave office buyers a different reason to visit the computer counter. The result was a week when the same store could sell cartridges, joysticks, educational programs, and spreadsheet power as parts of one expanding microcomputer habit.

computerItems.title: Commodore 64 keeps the memory headline
computerItems.summary: Early-1983 retail coverage continued to make the Commodore 64 a high-visibility home computer, selling 64K memory, color graphics, sound, and game potential against cheaper rivals.

computerItems.title: TI-99/4A keeps pressure on price
computerItems.summary: Texas Instruments stayed in the home-computer race with aggressive 99/4A pricing and rebate-era advertising that made the machine a frequent comparison point for family buyers.

computerItems.title: Lotus 1-2-3 gives the IBM PC counter a fresh sales hook
computerItems.summary: After going on sale in late January, Lotus 1-2-3 was still new enough in February to frame the IBM PC as a serious spreadsheet, charting, and database workstation.

computerItems.title: Computer Gaming World reviews keep strategy players browsing
computerItems.summary: The February 1983 Computer Gaming World issue shows a game market stretching beyond arcade conversions into wargames, adventures, and simulation titles for home computers.
